case_study_insert.main_stem: Citywide Cleaning Services (CCS) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, providing commercial and domestic cleaning with a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Marcus Bell, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CCS plans to invest $250,000 in a fleet of electric cleaning vans and eco-friendly equipment, financed by a $150,000 five-year bank loan and $100,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $96,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $50, and currently produces 8,400 units a year. CCS faces two problems: customer complaints about missed slots have risen and cleaner absenteeism has reached 11%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: CCS completed 2,100 cleaning jobs last quarter at a re-clean rate of 3.4%, down from 5.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 64 to 33 per month. Average response time to a new booking is 1.8 days. A survey of 500 households found that 66% would pay $6 more for eco-friendly cleaning and 59% choose a cleaner on reliability ratings. A training audit shows 18 of 60 cleaners have not completed on-the-job training on the new electric-van equipment; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $600 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Citywide Cleaning Services for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 8.2% from $13.96 to $15.10 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Fuel and eco-cleaning product input costs have risen 11.5% year-on-year, while household spending on cleaning services grew 3.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CCS plans to fund part of its $250,000 electric-van expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CCS of using retained profit to fund the $100,000 share instead of more bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or capital repayments, protecting CCS's cash flow while it already services a $150,000 bank loan and fixed costs of $96,000 a year. The saving helps absorb the 11.5% rise in fuel and eco-product costs without raising the $50 job price.

Point 2: Using $100,000 of retained profit avoids extra collateral and default risk, so the van fleet is not jeopardised if demand for cleaning jobs falls short of the 8,400-unit target. It also keeps Marcus Bell's ownership intact with no lender conditions on how the eco-friendly equipment is deployed.

Keeping $100,000 internal also gives CCS room to fund the $600 retraining for 18 cleaners and to absorb the 11.5% fuel rise without raising the $50 price and losing the 66% of households willing to pay $6 more. With revenue rising from $1,200,000 to $1,500,000, an internal contribution avoids adding a fixed repayment just as the van fleet adds fixed costs, leaving the 5,400-job margin of safety intact.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over bank borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CCS's expansion, loan and cost data.

questions.question_text: CCS is launching its new eco-friendly cleaning service. Consider local newspaper advertising, community radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should CCS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper ads reach households across CCS's city and can carry a coupon for the $6 eco-friendly premium, but readership is ageing, print costs are rising and response is hard to measure for a 60-staff firm funding a $250,000 van fleet.

Community radio sponsorship: Local radio is inexpensive and builds trust through repeated messages about reliability, reaching drivers and homeowners in the catchment. Its limit is narrow reach and no visual proof of the eco-friendly equipment, which may not generate the 8,400 jobs needed to cover $96,000 of fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Home and family influencers target exactly the 66% of 500 surveyed households who would pay $6 more for eco-friendly cleaning and the 59% who choose on reliability. Engagement is measurable and cost per lead is low, though results build gradually and depend on influencer credibility.

CCS's 2025 operating profit is $210,000, so a newspaper-scale spend would consume a noticeable share; influencer fees can be capped and judged against the $32 contribution per job and the 2,100 jobs completed last quarter. Print cannot demonstrate the electric vans, and radio's 1.8-day response message is easily forgotten; a visual, measurable campaign suits a 60-staff firm whose 42.0% gross margin leaves limited marketing headroom.

Recommendation: CCS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise survey segment, is cheaper than print and scales beyond a single radio catchment. Newspaper advertising is rejected as expensive and hard to track; community radio is rejected as too narrow and non-visual, so CCS should add reliability badges on the vans to convert the interest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to CCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CCS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in CCS's context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: CCS's complaint rate has risen and cleaner absenteeism has reached 11%. Explain two benefits for CCS of using autocratic leadership to improve performance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Marcus Bell set clear cleaning standards and strict slot times, giving quick decisions that cut the 3.4% re-clean rate and answer the customer complaints about missed slots. In a hierarchical structure of 60 staff, firm directives can be enforced fast.

Point 2: Tight control and close supervision directly target the 11% cleaner absenteeism through firm attendance rules and rapid replacement of no-shows, protecting the 8,400-job target and avoiding repeated $600 per employee retraining. Consistent standards also support the eco-friendly brand promised to customers.

Clear, top-down standards suit a 60-cleaner operation where missed slots drive complaints; Marcus Bell can set slot times that cut the 3.4% re-clean rate and protect the 42.0% gross margin. Firm attendance rules tackle the 11% absenteeism directly and reduce reliance on costly agency cleaners, whose wages would erode the $32 contribution per job. The approach must still heed customer feedback, since the 59% reliability effect depends on consistent, not merely fast, service.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CCS's complaints, absenteeism and output.

questions.question_text: CCS must upskill 18 cleaners to use the new electric-van equipment. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should CCS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Demonstrations on the actual vans are directly relevant to CCS's own equipment, cost no fees and keep all 18 cleaners working, protecting the 2,100 jobs completed last quarter and the fall in re-clean rate to 3.4%. Drawbacks are that supervisor-cleaners lose time, short cuts may be taught, and there is no certificate.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $600 per employee gives structured skills and a recognised certificate for 18 cleaners, costing $10,800 - minor against the $250,000 investment. It removes 18 of 60 staff from rounds, cutting capacity, and generic content may not match CCS's vans, so on-site practice would still follow.

The 18 cleaners needing training make up 30% of the 60-strong workforce, so a college course would remove nearly a third of capacity and worsen the 11% absenteeism and missed-slot complaints at launch. On-the-job demonstration on the actual vans keeps all 18 earning and protects the 2,100-job quarter. CCS should still log competence checks for insurance and quality, and can add the $600 college modules later from the $210,000 operating profit if standards demand certification.

Decision: CCS should choose on-the-job training, with brief college modules for team leaders. It is cheapest, equipment-specific and avoids losing capacity while absenteeism is 11%; full off-the-job training is rejected because a $10,800 fee and 18 cleaners off their rounds would worsen missed slots and complaints, and college sessions can be added once the fleet is embedded.

Spending $10,800 on one cohort would consume part of the $250,000 fleet budget, while on-the-job coaching can be repeated as new cleaners join without further fees.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in CCS's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in CCS's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CCS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $96,000 ÷ ($50 − $18) = $96,000 ÷ $32 = 3,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 3,000 cleaning jobs a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $50 − $18 = $32. Answer: contribution per unit is $32.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CCS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 3,000-job break-even point with 8,400 actual jobs, a margin of safety of 5,400, to judge whether the electric-van fleet is busy enough.
2. Use $32 contribution to test a $4 discount to $46, leaving $28 per job, still above the $18 variable cost while tackling the complaint-driven loss of customers.
3. Set job targets that service the $150,000 bank loan and justify the $250,000 fleet spend before Marcus Bell commits further capital.
4. Track average total cost of $29.43 ($96,000 ÷ 8,400 + $18) each quarter to spot re-clean waste and to check whether the 11.5% fuel-cost rise is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,000 jobs | (ii) Contribution per unit = $32 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety vs 8,400 jobs; discount modelling vs $96,000 fixed costs; loan servicing for the $250,000 fleet; and average total cost of $29.43 to monitor fuel inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid, contextual use in (iii) (max 4).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CCS's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CCS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 11.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $480,000 on revenue of $1,200,000 is 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $630,000 on revenue of $1,500,000 is 42.0%. Operating profit of $132,000 in 2024 equals 11.0% of revenue and 15.0% of the $880,000 capital employed; in 2025 operating profit of $210,000 is 14.0% of revenue and 17.5% of the $1,200,000 capital employed. Cost of sales rose from $720,000 to $870,000 but more slowly than revenue.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably. Gross margins widened from 40.0% to 42.0%, suggesting better control of labour and product costs; operating margins rose from 11.0% to 14.0%, so more of each fee becomes operating profit; and returns on capital employed increased from 15.0% to 17.5%, showing the enlarged asset base is generating more profit. Interest payable rose from $20,000 to $26,000, a small but growing burden, and an 11.5% fuel-cost rise could reverse the gross-margin gain.

Interest payable of $26,000 is modest against $210,000 operating profit, so financing does not overturn the improvement, but the 11.5% fuel-cost rise must be watched to defend the 42.0% gross margin.

Conclusion: CCS's financial position has improved on every permitted measure, and because margins and capital returns both rose the improvement is not just a revenue effect. The main risk is rising interest and fuel costs, so management should protect the 42.0% gross margin before the $250,000 van expansion adds more capital.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of margin, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CCS of offering the $6 eco-friendly cleaning premium identified in its survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Of 500 households surveyed, 66% would pay $6 more for eco-friendly cleaning and 59% choose on reliability, so the premium raises revenue per job and protects the $32 contribution even as fuel and product costs rise 11.5%. It also supports the new electric-van fleet's green brand.

Disadvantage: Price-sensitive households may reject the $6 premium, cutting the 8,400 jobs needed to justify the $250,000 vans and worsening missed-slot complaints. Eco-friendly products can cost more and, if supplies are unreliable, may raise the 3.4% re-clean rate and cleaner absenteeism already at 11%.

CCS should test the $6 premium in one district and track the 59% who choose on reliability, because eco-friendly claims must be credible or the brand suffers. A two-tier price could alienate households already complaining about missed slots, undercutting the 8,400-job target needed for the $250,000 vans. Part of the premium should fund the $600 retraining and reliable electric-van operation so the 42.0% gross margin is protected rather than merely charged.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CCS's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 8.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in fuel and cleaning input costs will affect CCS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If CCS's $150,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $150,000 = $1,125 a year, negligible beside $96,000 of fixed costs; a fixed loan removes even that. Higher rates may trim household discretionary cleaning spend, and CCS can cap the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (8.2%, to $15.10 an hour): With a workforce of 60, most cleaners are hourly-paid, so this is a large, unavoidable wage bill. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity - 8,400 jobs ÷ 60 cleaners = 140 jobs per worker - meaning the rise is bearable only if that productivity holds, otherwise the $32 contribution is squeezed.

Input cost inflation (11.5%): The $18 variable cost per job covers fuel and eco-products, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: a full 11.5% rise is 0.115 × $18 = $2.07 per job, about $17,388 a year at 8,400 jobs (8,400 × $2.07). Even a partial rise cuts contribution, and the $6 premium recovers only part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.5% rise in fuel and cleaning inputs has the greatest impact because it compounds over all 8,400 jobs and directly attacks the $32 contribution funding the $250,000 fleet; the wage rise is serious but manageable at 140 jobs per cleaner, and the interest rise costs at most $1,125 and can be fixed, so neither matches the input-cost shock.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to CCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on CCS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in CCS's context with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
